system.coreAbility:
Flourish. Show the beast that you mean business. Once
during your turn you may place 2 Threat on your area to
Feint as an immediate action. Feint is a special action only
available to Sword-wielders.
system.outlook:
The Sword is the King of Weapons. Ancient empires
rose and fell at its point. For millennia, the Sword has
been a symbol of power and authority beyond measure:

a tool for the masters of men to wield with skill and
grace. To cut away the weakest parts of society and to do
what must be done to ensure civilisation's survival and
prosperity.
Fate coalesces around the Sword's point. The Sword
makes myths. It rests in stones waiting for someone
deserving of the honour to rule the kingdom. It severs the
heads of tyrants and rests upon the right hands of great
men. It can elevate a common citizen to knighthood with
but a touch.
Next to the Sword, the frantic fear of the Knife and the
Spear fall away to nothing. The brutish Bludgeon falters
and stumbles. The Book is cut to shreds, the Staff sliced
in twain, the Armour rent asunder and the sound and fury
of the firearm silenced. It gladly bears the burden laid
upon its shoulders - someone's got to do it. Someone has
to lead the charge.
system.lies:
The Sword believes in heroes in the ancient sense of
the word. It wants to convince its wielders that they
stand proudly ahead of their peers: that there are those
who are born to lead, thanks to some indefinable spark of
greatness deep within their being, and it is their duty to
shepherd the people beneath them.
But the glorious ages of the past have died. The world
has grown sour and corrupt, and the concepts of which
the Sword sings - honour, duty, nobility and sacrifice -
are twisted and withered things. It spits hate on the
feckless masses and preaches exceptionalism. It tells you:
you alone are meant for greatness. These pitiful creatures
are nothing without you to lead them. You are worthy of
the respect you see glinting in their bovine eyes.
system.fears:
The Sword's time in the sun is over, and it clings to
what little relevance it retains. As the rifle and the
field gun scar the globe into new and terrible empires, the
Sword sees their eyes on the throne. It feels itself slipping
into rite and ritual as it becomes a relic of bygone days.
The Sword only matters if the people know it matters. Its
authority is not innate, but granted with conditions. Spears
outreach it. Knives carve and craft and make. It glances off
Armour's skin and every single gun outranges it.
So it speaks of honourable combat. It admonishes those
who fight dirty and births schools of duellists, manuals
of techniques, and reams of rules designed to fashion
the grim business of ending lives into something that
demands admiration and grace. It is desperate to dictate
the battlefield and hold onto its unfair advantage, because
without it, it is nothing but a length of sharpened steel.
